screens.title: The Evils of Duplication
screens.narratorSegment: Duplication is one of those small convenience choices that quietly becomes a large cost. In this lesson you will learn what the DRY principle really means: every piece of knowledge in a system should have one, unambiguous, authoritative representation. That includes not only repeated code, but duplicated data, configuration entries, documentation, and business rules. I will show concrete examples where copy‑paste or parallel implementations create a maintenance tax, and practical strategies to refactor duplication into reusable functions, a shared data model, or a single domain service. You'll see how small variations across copies lead to inconsistencies and bugs when rules change, and why a single source of truth reduces risk and improves agility. We will also practice a hands-on refactor where validation logic is extracted into a utility module and then re-used across routes. By the end, you should be able to find duplication, decide whether to refactor, and pick an appropriate technique that keeps readability and correctness high. Ask yourself as you work: where in your codebase is the same knowledge expressed more than once, and how would a single, well-named module improve future changes?

screens.title: What DRY Really Means
screens.narratorSegment: DRY stands for Don't Repeat Yourself, but the important part is its definition: every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system. Knowledge here means rules, data definitions, configuration, documentation, and algorithms. This is not a rule that says never write the same line twice; it's a rule about duplication of intent and meaning. For example, printing a simple log message in multiple places is typically not knowledge duplication, because the log itself doesn't represent business logic. By contrast, implementing the same discount calculation in two services is knowledge duplication because that calculation encodes a business rule that might change. A concrete example: suppose email validation logic appears in three route handlers each with slightly different regex or edge-case handling. That is a clear violation because email validity is business knowledge — it affects acceptance of users across the system. If the rule changes to accept new top-level domains, you must update every copy. A common misconception is treating every repeated line as DRY-violating; instead, ask whether a change to the underlying intent would require changing all copies. If yes, centralize it. Takeaway: centralize knowledge, not trivial repetition. Where would a single change require updates across files in your project?

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › What DRY Really Means
Definition
Every piece of knowledge has one authoritative representation
This includes logic, data models, configuration, and business rules. DRY reduces places a change must be made and avoids inconsistent behavior.
Concrete example
Email validation repeated in three handlers; centralize to a single is_valid_email function used everywhere.
Common misconception
Not every duplicate line is DRY-violation. Ask whether a change in intent requires changes across copies.
Key Takeaway

DRY protects knowledge, not trivial repetition. Centralize business rules and data definitions to keep behavior consistent.

Analogy
Imagine legal terms stored as copies in multiple contract templates. If law changes, you must update every template. Instead, reference a single clause so updates are reliable.
Check your understanding
  • Is a repeated log message a DRY problem? Only if the log encodes critical business meaning.
  • Does a single change require edits across files? If yes, centralize it.
Practical tip
When you identify duplication, write tests first for the behavior. Then extract the logic to ensure behavior remains unchanged after the refactor.

screens.title: Code vs Data vs Knowledge Duplication
screens.narratorSegment: Duplication appears in three distinct flavors and each has its own consequences and remedies. Code duplication is the most visible: identical or nearly identical code blocks scattered in multiple places. This is often fixed by extracting a function or creating a shared utility. A concrete example is three different email validation blocks using similar regex. Data duplication, on the other hand, stores the same information in multiple places, such as a user's address appearing in both a users table and an orders table. The fix here is designing a single source of truth through normalization and references. Knowledge duplication is subtler and often more dangerous. It happens when the same business rule or algorithm is implemented in separate layers or services. For example, if checkout and reporting each compute discounts independently, they may diverge. The right response is to codify the rule in one authoritative module or service and have all components call it. A common misconception is thinking only code duplication is harmful; in practice knowledge duplication causes inconsistent behavior and is harder to detect. Takeaway: match the remedy to the type — functions for code, SSOT for data, and central services or libraries for knowledge.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Code vs Data vs Knowledge
Comparison
How duplication types differ
Code duplication
Same or similar blocks. Fix by extracting functions, classes, or packages.
Data duplication
Same data stored in multiple locations. Fix with normalization and references to a single table or service.
Knowledge duplication
Business rules implemented in multiple places. Fix by centralizing logic into a single module or service.
Example
Email validation in three handlers is code duplication; storing address in two tables is data duplication; computing discounts in two services is knowledge duplication.
When to act
Prioritize refactors where a change in rules would require updates in multiple places. That signals knowledge or data duplication with high maintenance cost.
Common mistake
Rushing to abstract every repetition. Abstraction carries complexity; refactor gradually after demonstrating the need.
Check your understanding
Ask: If the rule changes, where will I need to edit? That question reveals the type and priority of duplication.

screens.title: Consequences of Ignoring DRY
screens.narratorSegment: Ignoring duplication is not just a stylistic problem; it has concrete, costly consequences. First, duplication multiplies maintenance work. A bug fix or a policy change must be applied in every copy, increasing time and the chance of mistakes. Second, inconsistent behavior emerges when one copy changes and others remain old. This leads to hard-to-find bugs because users experience different results depending on which code path runs. Third, duplication bloats the codebase. Redundant code makes the project larger and more intimidating for new contributors, raising the onboarding cost. Finally, duplication stifles innovation. When the same logic is spread across the system, developers fear changing it because the ripple effects are unknown. That results in a fragile codebase where small improvements are postponed. A common misconception is underestimating future cost: a quick copy‑paste saves minutes now but may add hours and bugs later. Practical approach: measure impact — how often the duplicated knowledge changes and how many places must be updated. High change frequency and many locations mean high priority for refactor. The takeaway: treat duplication as technical debt with predictable costs and prioritize refactors accordingly.

screens.title: A Practical Refactoring Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Refactoring duplication is best done with a simple, repeatable workflow. Start by detecting duplication through focused searches for repeated literals, similar regexes, or duplicated S Q L and by running code clone detectors. Once you identify a candidate, add tests that assert the current behavior. Tests are essential because they let you refactor with confidence. Next, extract the repeated knowledge into a single function, class, or service. Name it clearly so its intent is obvious — names are documentation. After extraction, replace the original copies with calls to the new central implementation and run the tests. Take small, reversible steps and keep commit history clear so you can revert if necessary. Finally, check for remaining edge-case differences; sometimes small differences are intentional and need parameterization rather than full unification. A common misconception is aiming for a one-off perfect abstraction. Instead, prefer iterative extraction and parameterization. Example: extract email validation to is_valid_email(email) and change each handler to call it. Does the behavior stay identical? Tests will tell you. A Practical Refactoring Workflow means add tests, extract a clear implementation, replace callers incrementally, and verify behavior remains identical.. In practical terms, detect duplication, add tests, extract, and replace incrementally. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Refactoring Workflow
Process
  1. Detect duplication using search and clone tools.
  2. Add tests that capture existing behavior.
  3. Extract the logic into a single, well-named module.
  4. Replace callers incrementally and run tests after each change.
  5. Parameterize differences rather than over-abstracting.
Example
Extract a password-check function used in registration and profile update routes, run tests, then replace both locations with the shared call.
Common mistake
Overcomplicating the extracted module. Keep the API minimal and clear. If it becomes complex, split responsibilities instead of creating a monster abstraction.
Check your understanding
After extraction, do tests pass? If not, examine differences in callers; those differences may need parameterization instead of full consolidation.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Starter Code
app.py (starter)
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
import re

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/register', methods=['POST'])
def register_user():
  data = request.get_json()
  email = data.get('email')
  password = data.get('password')

  # Duplicate email validation logic
  if not email or not re.match(r"[^@]+@[^@]+\.[^@]+", email):
    return jsonify({"error": "Invalid email format"}), 400

  # Duplicate password validation logic
  if not password or len(password) < 8 or not any(char.isdigit() for char in password):
    return jsonify({"error": "Password must be at least 8 characters and contain a digit"}), 400

  # Simulate user creation
  print(f"Registering user: {email}")
  return jsonify({"message": "User registered successfully"}), 201

@app.route('/update_profile', methods=['POST'])
def update_profile():
  data = request.get_json()
  email = data.get('email')
  password = data.get('password') # Password update is optional here

  if email:
    # Duplicate email validation logic
    if not re.match(r"[^@]+@[^@]+\.[^@]+", email):
      return jsonify({"error": "Invalid email format"}), 400

  if password:
    # Duplicate password validation logic
    if len(password) < 8 or not any(char.isdigit() for char in password):
      return jsonify({"error": "Password must be at least 8 characters and contain a digit"}), 400

  # Simulate profile update
  print(f"Updating profile for: {email if email else 'current user'}")
  return jsonify({"message": "Profile updated successfully"}), 200

if __name__ == '__main__':
  app.run(debug=True)
What to notice
Look for the two repeated validation blocks and consider naming and return contract for a shared validator.
Try this
Write tests for valid and invalid emails and passwords before you refactor.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › validators.py
validators.py (expected)
import re

def is_valid_email(email: str) -> bool:
  """Validates an email address format."""
  if not email or not re.match(r"[^@]+@[^@]+\.[^@]+", email):
    return False
  return True


def is_valid_password(password: str) -> bool:
  """Validates password strength requirements."""
  if not password or len(password) < 8 or not any(char.isdigit() for char in password):
    return False
  return True
Why this shape?
Boolean-returning functions are easy to call in conditionals and simple to test. Small, single-responsibility functions are easier to maintain.
Pro tip
Include concise docstrings describing the contract so other developers know expected input and behavior.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › app.py (refactored)
app.py (after refactor)
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
from validators import is_valid_email, is_valid_password

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/register', methods=['POST'])
def register_user():
  data = request.get_json()
  email = data.get('email')
  password = data.get('password')

  if not is_valid_email(email):
    return jsonify({"error": "Invalid email format"}), 400

  if not is_valid_password(password):
    return jsonify({"error": "Password must be at least 8 characters and contain a digit"}), 400

  print(f"Registering user: {email}")
  return jsonify({"message": "User registered successfully"}), 201

@app.route('/update_profile', methods=['POST'])
def update_profile():
  data = request.get_json()
  email = data.get('email')
  password = data.get('password')

  if email and not is_valid_email(email):
    return jsonify({"error": "Invalid email format"}), 400

  if password and not is_valid_password(password):
    return jsonify({"error": "Password must be at least 8 characters and contain a digit"}), 400

  print(f"Updating profile for: {email if email else 'current user'}")
  return jsonify({"message": "Profile updated successfully"}), 200

if __name__ == '__main__':
  app.run(debug=True)

  • Verify error messages and status codes are unchanged.

Forgetting to change all callers or leaving slightly different implementations in other places will defeat the refactor. Use search tools to find duplicates.

screens.title: Single Source of Truth (SSOT)
screens.narratorSegment: Single Source of Truth is a design principle closely linked to DRY when applied to data and business knowledge. SSOT means each data element or rule should be owned and updated in one place. For data, that often means normalizing storage and referencing a user record rather than copying address fields into orders. For business rules, SSOT implies a single module, library, or service that calculates the result and is called by interested parties. Consider discounts as an example: if the checkout service and reporting service each compute discounts independently, discrepancies arise. Instead, create a DiscountCalculator service with a clear A P I. Both checkout and reporting call it, and all changes occur in one place. A common mistake is centralizing logic in a way that couples unrelated modules tightly; the better approach is a small, focused A P I that expresses intent clearly. The takeaway is to design ownership and contract boundaries: who is authoritative for a piece of data or knowledge and how others request it? Single Source of Truth (SSOT) means define who owns each piece of data or rule and provide a clear, minimal api so all consumers use the authoritative implementation.. Architecture
Design authoritative owners

screens.title: When Not to DRY — Practical Limits
screens.narratorSegment: DRY is a guiding principle, not an absolute law. There are situations where trying to eliminate every repetition creates worse code. Over‑abstracting too early produces confusing APIs, brittle code paths, and increased complexity. The pragmatic approach is to refactor when duplication conveys knowledge that is likely to change or lead to bugs. If repetition is trivial or the cost of abstraction outweighs maintenance savings, it may be fine to leave it. A practical rule is to favor small, incremental refactors with tests over giant design changes. Also consider whether the duplicated code represents the same intent. If two similar blocks differ in meaningful ways, merging them could hide those differences and introduce subtle bugs. Example: identical loops that produce slightly different output depending on caller context might need parameterization rather than a single merging. The takeaway: aim to remove duplicated knowledge and intent, but keep readability and clarity first. In practical terms, avoid over-abstracting; prefer readable, maintainable solutions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Definition
Pragmatic limits of DRY
Not all repetition is harmful. Balance the cost of abstraction against long-term maintenance savings. Prefer incremental, tested refactors.
When to avoid DRY
If repetition is unlikely to change or abstraction would add significant complexity, keep duplication.
When to refactor
When duplicated knowledge affects correctness or will likely change, extract and centralize it.

Don't replace a simple repeated sentence with a complex macro unless it clearly reduces future work and improves clarity.

screens.title: Anti-patterns & Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: There are recurring anti-patterns you should watch for. Copy-paste is the most obvious: duplicating logic without extraction. Shotgun surgery describes a change that requires touching many files — a clear sign of duplicated knowledge. Premature abstraction is the opposite danger: trying to generalize before the need is clear, which creates complicated code and fragile tests. Recognize these by asking: does a single change require edits in many files? Do similar pieces differ in intent? When you find shotgun surgery, refactor to a single owner; when you find premature abstraction, roll it back or simplify the A P I. Another pitfall is hiding variations behind unclear parameters; prefer explicit, intention-revealing function names. Example: avoid a giant validate(input, flags) that behaves differently based on many flags. Instead, provide small, clearly‑named functions or composable validators. The takeaway is to be pragmatic: remove harmful duplication while keeping APIs simple and readable. After refactoring, run tests and document the new owner and contract so future developers know where to make changes. fullNarratorScript:
Duplication is one of those small convenience choices that quietly becomes a large cost. In this lesson you will learn what the DRY principle really means: every piece of knowledge in a system should have one, unambiguous, authoritative representation. That includes not only repeated code, but duplicated data, configuration entries, documentation, and business rules. I will show concrete examples where copy‑paste or parallel implementations create a maintenance tax, and practical strategies to refactor duplication into reusable functions, a shared data model, or a single domain service. You'll see how small variations across copies lead to inconsistencies and bugs when rules change, and why a single source of truth reduces risk and improves agility. We will also practice a hands-on refactor where validation logic is extracted into a utility module and then re-used across routes. By the end, you should be able to find duplication, decide whether to refactor, and pick an appropriate technique that keeps readability and correctness high. Ask yourself as you work: where in your codebase is the same knowledge expressed more than once, and how would a single, well-named module improve future changes?

By the end of the first objectives block you will be able to identify key forms of duplication and explain why they matter. Specifically, you will learn to spot copy‑paste code that repeats logic, recognize duplicated data stored in multiple tables or formats, and notice when similar business rules are expressed in separate services. I will give concrete checks you can run: search for repeated regexes, repeated S Q L columns, or duplicated calculation formulas. Knowing these signs helps you prioritize refactoring work and avoid fragile fixes that multiply problems. As you learn, keep an eye out for false positives. Not every repetition is harmful — basic patterns like logging calls or simple print statements are not knowledge duplication. The skill is distinguishing trivial repetition from duplicated knowledge that should be centralized. Practice with small examples and ask whether a change to one place would require coordinated changes everywhere else. This mental checklist will make your refactors safer and more impactful.

This second objectives screen shifts from detection to action and consequences. You will learn practical refactoring techniques such as extracting functions, creating a dedicated service for a business rule, and normalizing data to a single table. I will explain how to parameterize a shared routine so variations are handled without duplicating logic. Each technique includes when to apply it and a short example to practice. We will also examine the long-term costs when DRY is ignored: higher maintenance effort, inconsistent behavior across system paths, and bloated codebase that discourages change. You will practice small, safe refactors and learn a rule of thumb: refactor when a duplicated piece carries business meaning that is likely to change. Finally, you'll learn common pitfalls, particularly over‑abstracting early and premature generalization, and how to avoid them by iterating refactors and keeping code readable.

DRY stands for Don't Repeat Yourself, but the important part is its definition: every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system. Knowledge here means rules, data definitions, configuration, documentation, and algorithms. This is not a rule that says never write the same line twice; it's a rule about duplication of intent and meaning. For example, printing a simple log message in multiple places is typically not knowledge duplication, because the log itself doesn't represent business logic. By contrast, implementing the same discount calculation in two services is knowledge duplication because that calculation encodes a business rule that might change. A concrete example: suppose email validation logic appears in three route handlers each with slightly different regex or edge-case handling. That is a clear violation because email validity is business knowledge — it affects acceptance of users across the system. If the rule changes to accept new top-level domains, you must update every copy. A common misconception is treating every repeated line as DRY-violating; instead, ask whether a change to the underlying intent would require changing all copies. If yes, centralize it. Takeaway: centralize knowledge, not trivial repetition. Where would a single change require updates across files in your project?

Duplication appears in three distinct flavors and each has its own consequences and remedies. Code duplication is the most visible: identical or nearly identical code blocks scattered in multiple places. This is often fixed by extracting a function or creating a shared utility. A concrete example is three different email validation blocks using similar regex. Data duplication, on the other hand, stores the same information in multiple places, such as a user's address appearing in both a users table and an orders table. The fix here is designing a single source of truth through normalization and references. Knowledge duplication is subtler and often more dangerous. It happens when the same business rule or algorithm is implemented in separate layers or services. For example, if checkout and reporting each compute discounts independently, they may diverge. The right response is to codify the rule in one authoritative module or service and have all components call it. A common misconception is thinking only code duplication is harmful; in practice knowledge duplication causes inconsistent behavior and is harder to detect. Takeaway: match the remedy to the type — functions for code, SSOT for data, and central services or libraries for knowledge.

Ignoring duplication is not just a stylistic problem; it has concrete, costly consequences. First, duplication multiplies maintenance work. A bug fix or a policy change must be applied in every copy, increasing time and the chance of mistakes. Second, inconsistent behavior emerges when one copy changes and others remain old. This leads to hard-to-find bugs because users experience different results depending on which code path runs. Third, duplication bloats the codebase. Redundant code makes the project larger and more intimidating for new contributors, raising the onboarding cost. Finally, duplication stifles innovation. When the same logic is spread across the system, developers fear changing it because the ripple effects are unknown. That results in a fragile codebase where small improvements are postponed. A common misconception is underestimating future cost: a quick copy‑paste saves minutes now but may add hours and bugs later. Practical approach: measure impact — how often the duplicated knowledge changes and how many places must be updated. High change frequency and many locations mean high priority for refactor. The takeaway: treat duplication as technical debt with predictable costs and prioritize refactors accordingly.

Refactoring duplication is best done with a simple, repeatable workflow. Start by detecting duplication through focused searches for repeated literals, similar regexes, or duplicated S Q L and by running code clone detectors. Once you identify a candidate, add tests that assert the current behavior. Tests are essential because they let you refactor with confidence. Next, extract the repeated knowledge into a single function, class, or service. Name it clearly so its intent is obvious — names are documentation. After extraction, replace the original copies with calls to the new central implementation and run the tests. Take small, reversible steps and keep commit history clear so you can revert if necessary. Finally, check for remaining edge-case differences; sometimes small differences are intentional and need parameterization rather than full unification. A common misconception is aiming for a one-off perfect abstraction. Instead, prefer iterative extraction and parameterization. Example: extract email validation to is_valid_email(email) and change each handler to call it. Does the behavior stay identical? Tests will tell you. A Practical Refactoring Workflow means add tests, extract a clear implementation, replace callers incrementally, and verify behavior remains identical.. In practical terms, detect duplication, add tests, extract, and replace incrementally. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Now we will inspect a concrete example where duplication exists: a simple Flask application with registration and profile update routes that each contain email and password validation logic. Reading the code, notice identical or very similar regex checks and password rules repeated in both functions. The duplication here is both code and knowledge because the validation rules express business intent — what input we accept as valid. The correct refactor is to extract these rules into named functions so the logic is defined once and used everywhere. In the starter code you'll see the validation logic written inline twice. A common developer reaction is to quickly copy a working block into the new route. That saves minutes but makes future changes expensive and error-prone. DRY is a guiding principle, not an absolute law. There are situations where trying to eliminate every repetition creates worse code. Over‑abstracting too early produces confusing APIs, brittle code paths, and increased complexity. The pragmatic approach is to refactor when duplication conveys knowledge that is likely to change or lead to bugs. If repetition is trivial or the cost of abstraction outweighs maintenance savings, it may be fine to leave it. A practical rule is to favor small, incremental refactors with tests over giant design changes. Also consider whether the duplicated code represents the same intent. If two similar blocks differ in meaningful ways, merging them could hide those differences and introduce subtle bugs. Example: identical loops that produce slightly different output depending on caller context might need parameterization rather than a single merging. The takeaway: aim to remove duplicated knowledge and intent, but keep readability and clarity first. There are recurring anti-patterns you should watch for. Copy-paste is the most obvious: duplicating logic without extraction. Shotgun surgery describes a change that requires touching many files — a clear sign of duplicated knowledge. Premature abstraction is the opposite danger: trying to generalize before the need is clear, which creates complicated code and fragile tests. Recognize these by asking: does a single change require edits in many files? Do similar pieces differ in intent? When you find shotgun surgery, refactor to a single owner; when you find premature abstraction, roll it back or simplify the A P I. Another pitfall is hiding variations behind unclear parameters; prefer explicit, intention-revealing function names.
